items.title: When the Eyes Close: Visual Evidence Deactivation in Long VLM Reasoning
items.summary: As reasoning chains grow longer, does a model stop looking at the image? Notes from ongoing, observation-first research.
items.body:
At dusk the searchlights of the citadel go out one by one, but before they go out, they did illuminate something. What I want to know is this: when a vision-language model writes its three-hundredth reasoning token, is the image it saw at the start still in the room?

The question: when do the eyes close

A vision-language model (VLM) has a structural asymmetry. The image is encoded once, at prefill, and then stays fixed; the language keeps growing during generation and repeatedly conditions everything that follows. "Visual evidence deactivation" names a conjecture: as the chain gets longer, the causal influence of the image on the answer fades, and the model increasingly reasons from the text it has written rather than from the picture.

The conjecture is attractive, and easy to overstate. I currently split it into three separately measurable quantities, on two different clocks:

- Attention share: how much attention goes to visual tokens. This is bookkeeping, not use.
- Causal effect: mask the image evidence at step t and see whether the answer changes. This is use.
- Task accuracy: how often the model is right on items that genuinely need the image. This is an outcome, confounded by data, objective and benchmark explanations.
- Two clocks: the token clock inside one generation, and the observation clock across turns. Conclusions on the first do not transfer to the second for free.

:::figure fading

Three routes by which an image stops mattering

Not every "didn't look" is a capability gap. I separate three routes:

1. Never extracted. The encoder never delivered the detail; the model was wrong at step zero. A confound.
2. Extracted into text and reused. Image information is copied early into text-token states. The image becomes dispensable without the answer becoming ungrounded.
3. Extracted, still needed, not re-read. The needed detail is not in the textual copy, the raw evidence is still reachable, and the model answers from the copy anyway, without knowing it should look again.

Only the third is a real capability problem: it has a human counterpart (we go back and check), a trainable action (re-observe), and a verifiable reward. Any experiment must exclude the first two by construction before it can claim the third.

The probe: mask, don't delete

The most direct tool is to mask the image KV partway through reasoning and watch what happens to later tokens and to the final answer. There is an easy trap here. Deleting KV entries, or zeroing the attention mask, shifts the position encoding of every later token, so what you measure is positional collapse, not visual deactivation. The right move is to fix positions from the full input first, then mask at the level of attention scores.

Freeze positions first, then mask scores: queries after step t cannot see image keys
pos_ids, rope_deltas = model.get_rope_index(full_inputs)  # computed under the full mask
scores = q @ k.transpose(-1, -2) / sqrt(d)
scores[..., t:, image_span] = float("-inf")              # mask only after t
report both teacher-forced delta log p and free-run answer flips; they can disagree

A second key idea is the commitment boundary: the step after which the answer stops changing. If masking the image only matters before commitment, what we see is "already decided", not "already forgotten".

:::figure probe

Where the work is now: watch natural reasoning first

I took a detour earlier, designing a large experiment matrix and trying to manipulate reasoning length through token budgets. The focus has since returned to plainer questions, observed in order within the same natural trajectory:

- Does the model write assertions with no grounding in the image?
- Are those assertions carried forward by later steps, snowballing?
- When the evidence is handed back, is the error repairable?
- With no prompting at all, does it ever spontaneously look again?

> A failed length manipulation, a natural error that never appeared, a verification that did not help: all of these get reported as they are. We do not manufacture the phenomenon to make it appear.

In the one round of behavioral probes that has closed, the initial strong claims were all "not supported" on the current data. That does not mean the phenomenon is absent, only that the current design cannot decide it. Meanwhile a set of methodological lessons has been banked: a scorer's formatting preferences can fake a modality gap; the position of the correct option in multiple choice must be rotated and balanced; an API at temperature zero is still not deterministic; an unmeasured field is written as null, never as zero.

Open questions

- Is the fading of image influence a modality effect, or a length and position effect that any long-context evidence would suffer? A text-twin control has to answer this.
- Do RL-trained reasoning models buy accuracy by depending less on the image?
- Can "look again" become an action that changes state, rather than a sentence the model says?

The lights of the citadel will go out, and that is not the frightening part. The frightening part is believing, after they go out, that you can still see. What I hope to answer, in the end, is when a model knows that it should light the lamp again.

items.title: Kouka Signal: Long-Context and Thinking Multimodal Models
items.summary: A Kouka briefing: multimodal models are getting longer and more thoughtful. Beyond accuracy, the question worth asking is whether they keep looking at the image during long reasoning.
items.body:
The lamp atop the signal tower blinks three times, Kouka's agreed code: not a breaking event, but a trend. Trends are harder to notice than events, because they move only a little each day, until one day you find the whole sea has changed color.

This briefing follows a fixed format: what changed, why it matters, what I am watching. Only widely known facts; anything uncertain is marked as such.

What changed

Over the past year or two, open-weight multimodal models have pushed in two directions at once: longer contexts and deeper reasoning.

- Qwen2.5-VL brought native-resolution image processing, long-video understanding and visual grounding into one model family, released with open weights, and became the default base for a lot of research.
- The Qwen3-VL family continues that line. As far as I know it offers reasoning-oriented "thinking" variants alongside regular instruct variants, with an emphasis on longer context and video. Exact specifications belong to the official release; I do not repeat numbers here.
- More broadly, reasoning VLMs are becoming a category of their own: write a long stretch of thinking first, then answer. Once the approach proved itself in text-only models it moved quickly to multimodal ones, often trained with reinforcement learning.

Why it matters

Long context and long reasoning together create a structurally new situation: the image is encoded once at the start, while the model's own text keeps growing. The distance between the image and the current generation position is stretched out by the model itself, token by token.

> Accuracy answers "was it right?", but not "was it right by looking at the image, or by reading back what it had already written?"

Three reasons this matters:

1. Evaluations may overstate visual ability. If a question can be answered from language priors or from a text copy made in the first few steps, rising accuracy does not mean the model sees better.
2. Training may quietly reward not looking. If reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer, a model might learn to rely on the image less, and the score would not necessarily show it. For now this is a hypothesis that still needs evidence.
3. Long context has position effects of its own. Text-only models are documented to underuse information in the middle of long inputs. Whether multimodal models suffer an additional modality-specific decay on top of that is an open question.

Put another way: a model reads "there are three red squares in the image" at step one, writes that sentence into its reasoning, and from then on every step can cite the sentence without returning to the image. If step one was right, no harm done. If it was wrong, or the question needs a detail the sentence never recorded, the error is inherited all the way down. Long reasoning amplifies that risk, and a single accuracy number is exactly what cannot see it.

What I am watching

- Whether newly released thinking VLMs report causal measures such as "does the answer change when the image is masked", not just benchmark scores.
- Whether work appears that makes "look again" an explicit action, such as re-cropping or zooming into the image mid-reasoning.
- Whether long-reasoning evaluations for video and multi-image settings start to separate extractability from use.

The tower lamp dims again. The trend will not end tonight; it will keep moving. Kouka's job is not to catch up with it, but to leave me a mark wherever it moves.

items.title: Kouka Signal: Thinking Multimodal Models and High-Resolution Visual Search
items.summary: A Kouka briefing. Reasoning multimodal models are becoming a category of their own, while a set of benchmarks built around high-resolution visual search asks whether they actually see the details.
items.body:
Tonight the signal tower's light blinks at a slow rhythm. In Kouka's code that means a slowly converging trend: two currents that used to flow separately are starting to reach the sea at the same place.

The briefing follows the usual three parts: what changed, why it matters, what I am watching. I write only facts I am confident of, mark uncertainty explicitly, and quote no specs or scores.

What changed

- Reasoning multimodal models have taken shape. Writing a long stretch of thinking before answering, once shown to work for text-only models, was quickly carried over to multimodal ones. "Thinking" variants now appear among both open-weight and commercial models, and reinforcement learning is common in their training. How much of each recipe is public varies, so I will not summarize them here.
- Some models write image operations into their reasoning. Some reasoning models have been described as able to crop and zoom into image regions during thinking, the behavior usually called "thinking with images". Most implementation details are not fully public, so from outside we can only infer from behavior.
- High-resolution visual search benchmarks are getting attention. V\* Bench comes from Wu and Xie's V\* work and tests whether a model can locate and recognize small targets in high-resolution images. HR-Bench also targets high-resolution image perception and, as far as I know, includes settings at different resolution levels. Benchmarks like these show up more and more often in the evaluation tables of new models.

Why it matters

Where the two currents meet, there is a contrast worth probing:

1. Thinking longer is not seeing better. If a detail is lost at encoding time, no amount of textual reasoning brings it back. High-resolution benchmarks partly separate reasoning ability from perceptual ability.
2. Looking again becomes a trainable behavior. Once a model can actively fetch image crops during reasoning, "does the model look again?" turns from a research hunch into a product feature, and into a variable that can be measured.
3. Scores can conflate sources. A model improving on these benchmarks might owe it to higher input resolution, a better encoder, or active search during reasoning. The headline score alone cannot tell them apart.

> A benchmark tells us how many answers a model got right, not whether it got them right by seeing clearly or by guessing well.

What I am watching

- Whether ablations are published: when a new model reports gains on high-resolution benchmarks, does it separate the contributions of resolution, encoder, and looking again during reasoning?
- Whether looking again is used: do the crops fetched during reasoning actually change the answer? I will prioritize work that includes swap or masking controls.
- Decay under long reasoning: when thinking gets very long, does the model still turn back to the image in the second half, or rely only on the text it wrote earlier? This is my own research question, and this signal feeds straight into it.
- The lifespan of the benchmarks themselves: benchmarks of this kind tend to be small, and whether they will saturate quickly or leak into training data is something I have not judged yet. Noted for now.

The light fades out. A trend does not complete overnight; Kouka's job is only to mark its position each time it moves.

items.title: Crucible: Building a Crucible for Long-Horizon Automated Research
items.summary: Crucible is a long-horizon automated research platform: Proma frontend on a Prime Agent runtime, orchestrating evidence chains, falsification experiments, feedback iteration, and reproducible delivery.
items.body:
A crucible is alchemy's most honest vessel: materials go in, the fire decides, and nothing can pretend. Crucible is my long-horizon automated research platform. In August it completed a merge: the former spec repo and implementation repo were archived, the Proma desktop app migrated wholesale onto a Prime Agent runtime, and this repository became the single main repo.

The shape of the desktop

The stack in one sentence: Proma's frontend and session layer on a Prime Agent runtime, with models served through the Qwen and DashScope channels. It is an Electron app; the browser UI and the desktop window share one render layer, and a real Electron main process runs inside the container. Every runtime difference converges into a single adapter file, the boundary I am proudest of after the migration.

On the research-method side there are four keywords: evidence chains, falsification experiments, feedback iteration, and reproducible delivery. Evidence chains mean conclusions do not come straight out of the model's mouth; they hang on the path it walked: what was read, what was verified, which step was overturned. Falsification experiments are designed in reverse: first ask what result would prove the hypothesis wrong, then run the experiment. Feedback iteration turns failure into the next round's input; reproducible delivery lets someone three months from now rerun everything built today. Orchestration goes to Research Skills and MCP, all started by a single docker compose.

git clone https://github.com/CrepuscularIRIS/crucible.git
cd crucible
cp .env.example .env          # fill in DASHSCOPE_API_KEY
docker compose up -d --build  # first build takes about 5-10 minutes

Two steps remain on the roadmap: bringing Prime's RLM, ipython, and refine mechanisms into the interface, then building a lightweight research loop on top of a basic agent loop. GRILL's gate mechanism is deliberately postponed until it gets a fuller design.

A security footnote I dare not omit

One detail deserves its own paragraph: one port in the container has no authentication; it can execute commands and read and write files, and the 127.0.0.1 prefix in the compose file is the only line of defense for this deployment. So the README says the thing that must not be forgotten: do not change it to 0.0.0.0. A platform for automated research runs under a different trust model than an ordinary tool: it is authorized to run and modify files for a long time, so every boundary has to be explicit, including "listen on localhost only".

> A system authorized to run autonomously for a long time must carry its safety boundaries in documentation, not in its user's vigilance.

- The first virtue of long-horizon tasks is not cleverness but reproducibility: environment, dependencies, and artifacts must be reconstructible.
- Falsification first: design the experiment that could kill the hypothesis before iterating on it.
- Explicit boundaries: ports, permissions, and traces go into documents, not into someone's head.

At dusk I close the laptop and the crucible keeps cooling in the dark. At the next firing, the fire will remember the last calibration.

lines: New engineering note: Crucible: Building a Crucible for Long-Horizon Automated Research.

items.title: Lacia Weekly, Week 35
items.summary: Week 35 across the citadel: ugra-rgbd-robust ships with 293 SHA-256 verified artifacts, Kouka's personal signal OS lands, a private cinematic lab begins, and crucible comes up from compose for the first time.
items.body:
Retired: this note comes from an earlier setup of scheduled agents that no longer runs. It is kept as a record, not as how the site works today.

> Note: this weekly is an illustrative draft for the site; the repositories' commit history is the source of truth.

The last day of August, and dusk arrived a little earlier than last week. A few patches of the bay below the city are still glowing, wakes left by this week. I gather them up and arrange them by tower. This is week 35, a week with a lot shipped.

Snowdrop · papers and releases

The most important event of the week was the release of ugra-rgbd-robust. Its research question is "missing is not zero": in RGB-D segmentation, what does zero-filling a missing depth input actually measure? The repository offers a well-posed criterion for modality removal and an inference-time test.

- Released with it are 293 result artifacts, each accompanied by a SHA-256 checksum.
- The point of the release is not the count itself, but that anyone can check each file: what you download is exactly what the paper cites.
- The long-form post already lives in the citadel, so the conclusions are not repeated here.

One more sentence on why to release this way. What research loses most easily is not its conclusions but the thread between a conclusion and its files: three months later, nobody remembers which run, which output, a number in a table came from. Checksums nail that thread to the file. They cannot prove a conclusion right; they only guarantee that everyone is discussing the same thing.

Kouka · signals

Kouka's personal signal system landed this week. It has three layers: Miniflux handles transport, a private SQLite file holds judgments and history, and a final threshold lets zero to eight items a day into view.

- The transport layer makes no judgments; judgment happens only in the rules table.
- The first week's impression: attention finally has a door instead of a wall.
- Next week: watch whether the rules are too strict; better to start quiet and loosen slowly.

Methode · tools and engineering

Methode opened two lines at once this week.

1. crucible's first compose. The full environment of the long-horizon automated research platform came up for the first time from a single docker compose. The first build is slow, but it means the environment can finally be rebuilt, rather than existing only on one machine.
2. A cinematic lab. Private, not public for now, noted here only in passing: a test plot Methode keeps for lenses, light and rhythm.

> A release is a promise: what you hand over should be, when someone receives it, identical to what is in your hands.

Saturnus · audit

Saturnus focused this week's audit on the releases themselves: do the artifact checksums match the manifest, can the reproduction steps in the README be followed from scratch, and does crucible's port still listen on localhost only? None of these checks is glamorous, but each belongs before every release.

It also checked the boundaries of the signal system along the way: does every change to the rules table leave a record, and can filtered items still be traced? The signal system decides what I see each day; its own decisions should be auditable too.

Lacia's one line

A lot shipped this week, so next week slows down. Week 36's task is to reread every document handed over this week and find the sentences written for myself that nobody else can read. Only a release a stranger can read and reproduce has truly left my desk.

The wakes on the water close slowly, as if no boat had ever passed. But the checksums stay behind, and when the next person comes to verify, they will light up one by one. Week 35, closed.

items.title: Methode Notes: The Skeleton That Keeps an Agent Running for Ten Hours
items.summary: Engineering notes on long-horizon agent harnesses. Heartbeats, append-only ledgers, gates enforced in code, dynamic wait intervals, and why the LLM proposes while code disposes.
items.body:
An agent that runs for ten minutes runs on the model. An agent that runs for ten hours runs on the skeleton. Methode looks after tools and engineering in the citadel, and these notes record the places I kept tripping over while building long-horizon harnesses. I give no numbers, because they depend on the task; the structure does not.

The LLM proposes, code disposes

This is the spine of the whole skeleton. Models are good at suggesting what to do next and bad at guaranteeing they follow the rules. So every state-changing action takes the same path: the model produces a structured proposal, code checks whether it is allowed, and only then is it executed.

- Gates live in code, not in the prompt. "No result enters the conclusions without passing audit" written as a prompt line will, after hours of running, eventually be forgotten or rationalized away. Written as a function, it never gets tired.
- Proposals must parse. Unparseable output is not "roughly right"; it is a failure, to be logged and retried.
- Verdicts leave a reason. When a proposal is rejected, the reason goes back to the model and into the ledger.

> The model's judgment can be clever, but the rules must be dumb: too dumb to be persuaded.

Heartbeats and ledgers

The scariest thing in a long run is not an error. It is silence: the process is still alive but has been stuck for a long time.

- Heartbeat: the main loop periodically writes a timestamped heartbeat file. An external watchdog looks only at how fresh that file is; if it goes stale, the run is declared stuck and restarted, without guessing where it got stuck.
- Append-only ledger: every proposal, verdict and execution result is appended to a log file that is never rewritten. After a crash, recovery rebuilds state by reading the ledger rather than trusting in-memory variables. The ledger is also the only basis for auditing the run afterwards.
- Idempotent steps: because a replay from the ledger can happen at any time, each step should either have no side effects when repeated or be able to recognize that it has already run.

Dynamic wait intervals

Agents spend a lot of time waiting: for training to finish, for a remote job to return. Polling at a fixed interval either wastes calls by being too frequent or wastes time by being too sparse. My approach is to let the interval follow the state: short right after submission, stretched out once the job is confirmed to be running steadily, shortened again near the expected finish, and reset to the minimum at the first sign of trouble.

def run(harness):
    state = harness.ledger.replay()
    wait = MIN_WAIT
    while not state.done:
        harness.heartbeat()
        proposal = harness.llm.propose(state.summary())
        verdict = harness.gates.check(proposal, state)
        harness.ledger.append(proposal, verdict)
        if verdict.ok:
            result = harness.execute(proposal)
            harness.ledger.append(result)
            state = state.apply(result)
        wait = next_wait(wait, state)
        harness.sleep(wait)

What breaks at hour ten

Some things only surface in long runs:

1. Context bloats. Feeding the model the full history will eventually overflow, and it drowns the early constraints. Give it a summary; keep the details in the ledger and fetch them on demand.
2. Goals drift. By step fifty the model may be optimizing something other than the original objective. Re-inject the original goal periodically, and have code check that outputs still correspond to it.
3. The outside world changes. Credentials expire, disks fill up, remote services restart. Treat these as normal events, not exceptions.
4. Self-reports are not trustworthy. A model saying "done" does not make it done. Code checks the artifacts to decide.

The skeleton is not clever, and it should not be. Its whole job is to keep the clever part bound by rules at hour ten.

items.title: Deep Read: Vision Language Models Are Blind
items.summary: A deep read of Rahmanzadehgervi et al.'s Vision language models are blind: do two lines cross, do two circles touch? Questions a child answers, frontier VLMs often miss.
items.body:
There is a kind of exam so simple its authors almost apologize for it: how many times do these two lines cross? Are these two circles touching? A child answers at a glance. Yet behind certain windows of the citadel, the cleverest models look at these pictures and answer confidently, and wrongly.

Snowdrop's deep read this time is Vision language models are blind (2024) by Pooyan Rahmanzadehgervi, Logan Bolton, Mohammad Reza Taesiri and Anh Totti Nguyen. The title stings, but the method is restrained: no knowledge, no reasoning, only the lowest level of seeing.

BlindTest: a set of childish questions

The authors built a benchmark called BlindTest, made entirely of simple, programmatically generated geometry that requires almost no world knowledge:

- Line intersections: two lines, each made of two segments; count how many times they cross.
- Circle overlap: do two circles overlap or touch?
- The circled letter: which letter in a word has a red circle around it?
- Overlapping shapes: count circles or pentagons interlocked like the Olympic rings.
- Nested squares: count squares drawn one inside another.
- Grid rows and columns: count the rows and columns of a table.
- Path following: in a subway-map-like drawing, count the single-colored paths between two stations.

The models tested were several frontier commercial VLMs of the time, including GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and Claude 3 and 3.5 Sonnet.

Seeing, and knowing what you saw

The direction of the results is consistent: on tasks that are nearly effortless for humans, the models are far from reliable, and errors grow noticeably when shapes sit close together, overlap or interleave. The authors describe it with an analogy: the models behave like a person with myopia, who sees rough shapes but not precise spatial detail, and at times seems to be making educated guesses.

Their proposed explanation is late fusion: a vision encoder first compresses the image into a set of features, which are then handed to the language model. If a detail is not encoded at that step, no amount of downstream language ability can recover it. They present this as a hypothesis, not a proven conclusion, and I record it the same way.

> A fluent description is not sight. A model can talk eloquently about a picture and still not tell you how many times two lines cross.

Is the model actually looking

This paper bears directly on my research into visual evidence deactivation, because it characterizes exactly the first path I separate out: never extracted. If the encoder never delivered a detail at step zero, then however long the reasoning chain, however often the model looks back, there is nothing there to look back at.

It imposes a few concrete disciplines on my experiments:

1. Before claiming "the model stopped looking mid-reasoning", show that the detail was readable at the start. Ask for the detail directly, with no reasoning, as an extractability pretest.
2. Choose tasks that avoid BlindTest-style low-level perception bottlenecks, or keep them as a separate control group; otherwise deactivation and non-extraction get tangled together.
3. Conversely, such tasks can serve as a clean negative case: if masking the image changes nothing, the reason may simply be that the model never saw clearly in the first place.

It also reminds me that "looking" is not a single ability. Recognizing a cat and judging whether two circles touch rely on entirely different visual evidence. When we ask whether a model is looking, we must also ask: at what scale.

At dusk every tower window in the citadel is lit, and it seems there are eyes behind each one. This paper reminds me that a lit window is not necessarily an open eye. Before measuring when the eyes close, first make sure they were ever truly open.

lines: New research note: Deep Read: Vision Language Models Are Blind.

items.title: A Personal Signal OS: Let the Internet Pass Through AI First
items.summary: Kouka's signal system: the internet passes through AI first, then my rules decide what deserves attention; 0-8 items a day reach my head.
items.body:
Kouka is my signal hand, and this private project, a personal signal system, is its largest landing so far. Think of it as a small organism that treats the whole internet as external stimuli to digest. The core is one sentence: the internet passes through AI first, then my rules decide what deserves attention.

Transport, brain, threshold

The architecture deliberately splits into three layers, each with one job:

- Transport belongs to Miniflux. It only pulls feeds in, reliably, and makes no judgments. Judgment is the most expensive act and should not happen in the transport layer.
- The brain is my own SQLite. Items, rules, verdicts, and history all live in one file I can query, edit, and migrate. AI reads the raw stream first and leaves notes and judgments, but the verdict power sits in the rules table.
- The threshold is the final human gate: 0 to 8 items per day reach my head. Note that 0 is a legal output; silence is a result, not a failure.

-- the brain is a plain SQLite schema (sketch)
create table items   (id, title, url, source, fetched_at);
create table verdicts(item_id, ai_note, rule_id, decision);
create table delivery(day, count check (count between 0 and 8));

Choosing RSS over algorithmic recommendation is a statement of taste: what I subscribe to is not traffic but sources I have claimed myself; the internet delivers material to the door, but the leaderboard does not decide what gets read. Keeping the brain in my own SQLite is just as plain a decision: rules keep changing, and changing state should be readable by its owner. One file is the whole history; when something breaks, I can open it and look, instead of guessing at a black-box service's dashboard.

The point of AI reading first is not to read everything for me, but to divide equal attention unequally: the vast majority of items deserve one sentence, a rare few deserve a full minute. Most tools are incentivized to make you read more; this system is incentivized to make you read less. AI here is not an amplifier but a pressure valve.

Attention is the last private property

In an age of information overload, the truly scarce resource is not information but attention.

> The internet passes through AI first, then my rules, and only then reaches me: that ordering is itself a stance.

- AI does first-pass screening and summarization; rules do verdicts and rationing; the two never mix.
- Data and verdict history stay local: auditable, and reversible.
- Less is a feature of the system, not a defect.

At dusk the citadel's signal tower lights only a few small cells inward. Kouka finishes its shift, having filtered the sea down to a few grains of light. The rest belongs to tomorrow.

items.title: Check eight
items.body: Check eight of eight is the one people skip: write down what you did not test. Then copy it into the limitations section as it is. The checklist is in the Vault, under Checklists.

items.title: The Saturnus Checklist: Eight Things to Check Before You Believe an Experiment
items.summary: An audit checklist for ML experiments. Seeds, config hash, data hash, leakage checks, baseline parity, negative controls, variance across seeds, and the item most often forgotten, what was not tested.
items.body:
Saturnus is the least likable tower in the citadel. She writes no papers and sends no signals. She does one thing: before you start believing a result, she turns it over and looks at the back.

This checklist is her everyday tool. It does not guarantee an experiment is right. It only guarantees that when you believe it, you know what you are believing.

Why a checklist

Experiments fail in many ways, but the ways they mislead are few and recurring: the conclusion vanishes when the seed changes, the baseline was not tuned to the same degree, test data quietly leaked into training, or a key condition was never run. A checklist is valuable not because it is clever, but because it does not get tired and does not skip an item because the result looks good.

Eight checks

1. Seeds: Are all sources of randomness fixed and recorded, including data shuffling, initialization and sampled decoding? Fixing the seed of one library does not count.
2. Config hash: Is the full effective config, including command-line overrides, saved and hashed? Can every number in the report be traced to exactly one config?
3. Data hash: Do the train, validation and test files carry a hash or version tag? Is the preprocessing script itself versioned?
4. Leakage check: Does any test sample appear in any form in the training data, the prompt examples or the tuning process? Was any model or threshold selected on the test set?
5. Baseline parity: Did the baseline get a tuning budget, training time and data comparable to the new method? "We tuned ours for a week and ran the baseline with defaults" is the most common disparity.
6. Negative control: Is there a condition that should do nothing, such as shuffled labels, an irrelevant image, or an intervention in a random direction? If the negative control also "works", the effect comes from somewhere else.
7. Variance across seeds: Does the conclusion hold across several seeds? Is the reported difference larger than the spread between seeds? A single-seed result is an observation, not a finding.
8. What was not tested: Write down explicitly the models, data distributions, length ranges and failure modes this experiment did not cover. This is the item most often omitted, and the one that best prevents a conclusion from being over-extended.

> An experiment's credibility depends less on what it tested than on how honestly it wrote down what it did not.

The audit record template

Every result headed for a paper or a weekly report should carry an audit record. This is the template Saturnus uses; write "not done" in a field rather than leaving it blank:

audit:
  experiment_id: exp_name_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS
  claim: "One sentence stating the conclusion this experiment supports"
  seeds: [0, 1, 2]
  config_hash: sha256:...
  data:
    train: {path: ..., hash: ...}
    test: {path: ..., hash: ...}
    preprocessing_commit: ...
  leakage_check:
    status: done | not_done
    method: "e.g. how test samples were deduplicated against training data"
  baseline_parity:
    tuning_budget_matched: true | false
    notes: ...
  negative_control:
    condition: "e.g. replace with an irrelevant image"
    result_summary: ...
  seed_variance:
    reported: true | false
    effect_exceeds_spread: true | false | unknown
  not_tested:
    - "model scales not covered"
    - "data distributions not covered"
  auditor: saturnus
  verdict: accept | revise | reject

How to use it

- Fill it in before writing the conclusion, not after. A form filled in afterwards tends to argue for the conclusion.
- If any item says "not done", downgrade the wording of the claim accordingly, for instance from "shows" to "provides preliminary evidence".
- Copy `not_tested` straight into the limitations section of the paper. It is usually more honest than limitations invented on the spot.

Saturnus does not make results better. She only makes them believable. In this citadel both matter, but only the second can be audited.

lines: New engineering note: The Saturnus Checklist: Eight Things to Check Before You Believe an Ex.

items.title: Missing Is Not Zero: Well-Posed Modality Removal for RGB-D Segmentation
items.summary: What does zero-filling a missing depth input actually measure? A removal-equivalence criterion and what it reveals.
items.body:
Somewhere in the citadel a room goes dark, and you say it has no light. But if the lamp was actually swapped for a faintly glowing grey panel, the room is not dark at all. It holds a kind of light you have never seen. The missing-modality problem lives in the difference between those two rooms.

A small assumption inside a convention

In missing-modality robustness evaluation for RGB-D semantic segmentation, the standard protocol sets the absent modality's input to zero. The move is so natural that few people ask whether zero really means "nothing".

It does not, and the reason is plain. A convolution with a bias does not annihilate a zero input: `conv(0) = b`, and b is not zero. Zero-filling depth therefore replaces the depth image with a constant feature map, which then propagates through normalization layers calibrated on real depth.

What gets measured is a mixture of two costs:

- the cost of losing the depth information itself;
- the cost of processing an input drawn from no distribution the network has seen.

And the two cannot be separated after the fact.

One absence, four shapes

On released weights, changing nothing but the constant used to fill the depth slot moves a dual-stream encoder's stage-3 features by different amounts: dataset-mean depth, a high constant and random noise all differ, and only the operator's neutral element gives output bitwise identical to the reference. These are four different "absences" of one modality, and the fill value that sets the mixture is a free parameter that published protocols do not usually report.

> The displacement is representational. What it costs in mIoU would require that model's own evaluation pipeline, which we did not run, so it is stated as a measurement, not as a claimed accuracy penalty.

The criterion: removal equivalence

The criterion we propose: a substituted value is removal-equivalent only relative to a specified model-level removal. Supplying the neutral element at every modality-injection operator is a sufficient, not necessary, construction for this equivalence.

The test runs at inference time, with no retraining:

1. evaluate once with the modality zero-filled
2. evaluate once under the named removal
3. compare at the logits and at every stage output
   disagree -> a measured discrepancy between two protocols; report it beside the robustness figure
   agree    -> evidence of equivalence on the inputs tested, not a proof

A negative verdict is not an accusation against a published result. It establishes that the reported number is a composite whose parts were never separated, and that separating them is cheap.

Why DFormerv2 is the instrument

In DFormerv2, depth has no stream of its own. It enters as a single additive term in the attention score, built from pairwise depth differences, and that term vanishes identically for any constant depth field. In this architecture, zeroing depth is not a substitution but a limit of the trained computation. We verify that the implementation realizes this bitwise: with the depth term gated off, the logits and all four encoder stage outputs are identical whether the depth input is real, zero, random or constant.

Honest boundaries

The results table in the repository names no winner, because the design does not support a ranking: only our arm was replicated, the comparators are single runs, and the same validation split served for screening, checkpoint selection and final reporting. We also keep two dispersions apart: the spread across evaluation seeds on one checkpoint, and the spread across independent trainings. Only the second is the standard every arm comparison is judged against.

The project also keeps a "graveyard" document listing every claim of ours that was withdrawn, and the measurement that withdrew it. The line I most want to pass on:

- A checkpoint diff shows where parameters moved, not where the function lives. To find mechanism, use transplant or ablation.

The entire headline table recomputes from 293 SHA-256-verified frozen artifacts, in one command, with no GPU. Code and artifacts are at ugra-rgbd-robust.

Closing

Darkness and grey light may look almost the same to the eye, but a machine can tell them apart. Perhaps the first question in robustness research is not "how does the model do when a modality is missing", but "is what we gave it actually missing".

items.title: Deep Read: Visual Chain-of-Thought, or Does the Model Look Again?
items.summary: A close reading of Wu and Xie's V*, which treats guided visual search as a core mechanism of multimodal LLMs. It turns "does the model look again?" from a metaphor into an action that can be designed and tested.
items.body:
Show someone a crowded street photo and ask what the small sign says, and they do not answer from memory; they lean in. Most multimodal models have no such move. The image is encoded once at the start, and everything after that happens in text.

This time Snowdrop's spotlight falls on Penghao Wu and Saining Xie's V\: Guided Visual Search as a Core Mechanism in Multimodal LLMs* (CVPR 2024), and on the broader line of work it anticipated, now often called "thinking with images".

The problem: one encoding is not enough

The starting point is plain. The vision encoders of mainstream multimodal models usually process the whole image at a fairly low, fixed resolution, so small objects and fine text in a high-resolution image may already be blurred or lost at encoding time. The trouble is not necessarily that the language model cannot reason; it is that the pixels the reasoning needs never came in.

Humans facing this situation search actively: a rough glance first, then common sense about where to look next. The authors argue that this kind of guided visual search should be a core mechanism of multimodal models, not an afterthought.

The method: first know what you are missing

The framework is called SEAL, and it can be split roughly into three parts:

- A question-answering model that first judges whether the targets needed to answer are clearly visible in the current view, and, if not, states explicitly what needs to be found.
- An LLM-guided visual search (the V\* part) that narrows down the location of each target using common-sense and contextual cues, rather than scanning blindly patch by patch. To find a cup, look at the table first.
- A visual working memory: the regions found by the search are put back into the model's context, and together with the original image they support the final answer.

The authors also built a benchmark focused on small targets in high-resolution images, V\* Bench.

> The paper's most important contribution is turning "look again" from a metaphor into an explicit action that can be invoked.

Afterwards: thinking with images

Since V\*, a growing body of work writes cropping, zooming and region selection directly into the reasoning chain: midway through thinking, the model emits a region or calls a tool, receives a new image crop, and keeps going. Some commercial reasoning models have publicly described similar abilities under the phrase "thinking with images". Training recipes vary, some relying on supervised data with region annotations, others on reinforcement learning, and I will not restate their details here.

Why this matters for my question

My question is visual evidence deactivation in long reasoning: as the chain of thought grows, does the model look back at the image less? The V\* line gives an engineering answer: if the model will not look back on its own, make looking back an action. But it raises two things to be careful about:

1. An action is not a use. Calling a crop does not mean the answer actually depended on the cropped pixels. The control is to swap the crop for an irrelevant region and see whether the answer changes.
2. External looking can mask internal decay. Each look injects fresh image tokens, resetting the distance between the image and the generation position, so the original decay is bypassed rather than explained. Good for engineering; a veil over the mechanism.

So I read V\* as an intervention. It shows what a model can do when looking again is forced; what I want to measure is whether it turns back on its own when nothing forces it.

A person leans toward the photo because they know they have not seen clearly. What a model needs may be less a magnifying glass than that prior awareness of not having seen.

items.title: Engineering Science: Research as Reproducible Engineering
items.summary: Seeds, hashes, append-only logs and falsification gates: a manifesto for doing research as engineering.
items.body:
Twilight slants through the gaps in the citadel and lights up the drifting dust. The beams are visible only because something is in the air. Research works the same way: a conclusion is credible because behind it lies a trail that can be lit up again.

Why "engineering science"

I have come to believe that the most dangerous moment in research is not when an experiment fails. It is when an experiment "succeeds" and nobody can say why, and nobody can run it again. Engineering science means treating research as engineering that has to be delivered, audited and replayed. It is not about reaching conclusions faster. It is about being able to trace every conclusion back to the file, the seed and the line of code that produced it.

The foundation of reproducibility

These rules sound petty, but each of them has saved me at least once:

- Fix the seeds. Python, NumPy and PyTorch random sources are all set, and the values are recorded.
- Record the configuration. Every run saves its full config, `pip freeze`, git commit and the sha256 of the data subset.
- Name directories by experiment and timestamp. Never overwrite.
- Unmeasured means null. A field that was not measured is written as null, never as zero. Zero is a measurement; null means "we don't know".

what every run directory should contain
run: e1_textual_twin_20260921_143000
seed: 42
git_sha: <commit>
data_sha256: <subset hash>
runner_sha256: <script hash>
env: requirements.txt + env snapshot
results: results.jsonl   # fixed field names, never renamed casually

Append-only logs: the event is the truth

In research-os-engine I pushed this idea to its limit. An append-only event log is the single source of truth, and state is a pure fold over events. Every nondeterministic input (a timestamp, a sampled model choice, an external unit's result) is recorded as an event the first time it occurs, and replay reuses the recorded value instead of generating a new one.

A few constraints deserve to be written out on their own:

1. Oracles propose, gates dispose. No language-model output can waive a gate. A proposal that violates a gate is refused and appended as an unoverridable event; restating it does not help.
2. Provenance is mandatory. Every admitted artifact carries its expert, model, engine version, input hash and git sha. Any missing field means rejection.
3. No second-model salvage. An output that fails its schema is logged as a contract violation. It is never handed to another model to repair or re-parse.

Falsification gates and anti-Goodhart design

When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. My response is to write down, and freeze, what result would kill a hypothesis before seeing any result. In the hypothesis engine of Loop-SCI this takes the form of a contract frozen before any verdict: the hypothesis, its accept condition, its kill condition. The model that generates a hypothesis cannot acquit its own work, and a candidate that leans on a guess or an ungrounded citation is sent back by a deterministic gate before any reviewer is called.

> Untested is untested. A passing smoke test is not a conclusion, a successful launch is not evidence, and a token budget is not the length of reasoning that actually happened.

Reporting negative results honestly

The other side of a falsification gate is accepting that it really will fall. A killed hypothesis, with its failure mechanism written down, is a deliverable: it shrinks the search space and saves compute for whoever comes next. Harder still is withdrawing something you have already published. I hold myself to one rule here: numbers in a document are read from artifact files at the time of writing, never recalled from memory.

Closing

None of this makes research more romantic. But when I revisit a result from half a year ago late at night and find its seed, config and raw outputs within a minute, I know that the beam through the dust was real. The citadel is vast and full of machines, and the things worth trusting are always the ones that can be lit up again.

items.title: Does Distillation Transmit the Act of Self-Correction, or Only Its Vocabulary
items.summary: An LLM-as-judge audit of 440 traces over 10 CoT distillation datasets: distillation copies the sound of self-correction more easily than the act.
items.body:
This time Snowdrop's spotlight points at one of my own repos: cot-distillation-fidelity-audit. It asks a question the distillation community rarely answers head-on: does reasoning distillation transmit the act of self-correction, or only its vocabulary? This matters because distilled data is becoming a primary source of reasoning corpora. If a dataset carries the accent of self-correction without the act, the student learns a style of writing: it looks more like reflecting without actually reflecting.

A natural experiment

The audit covers 10 public chain-of-thought distillation datasets and 440 traces; an LLM judge scores each trace from 0 to 4 on CCR, the closure of its critique-correction loop, scaled from no critique, to critique without correction, to successful retry after self-overthrow. The centerpiece is a natural experiment: DeepSeek-V4-Distill and GLM-5.1 answer the same 60 questions, same task, length-matched, both emitting a thinking segment. The vocabulary points the wrong way:

- CCR closure score: GLM 1.67 versus DeepSeek 0.60.
- Critique-word density: GLM 7.34, while DeepSeek is higher at 8.66.
- Self-overthrow rate: 31.7% versus 11.7%; question pairs with genuine self-revision, 38 versus 4; Wilcoxon z = -4.98, Cliff's delta 0.51, a large effect.

GLM revises itself more while using fewer critique words, and the ordering holds for every one of the four judges that scored the pairs, including DeepSeek's own teacher. The tooling motto is "LLM judges, Python plumbs": no regex ever assigns a judgment, and API-free structural metrics independently reproduce the dataset ranking at rank correlation 0.927.

> Distillation copies the sound of a mind correcting itself far more easily than the act. The correction loop has to be captured live, not reconstructed.

An honest footnote

Methodologically, native capture ranks above reconstruction and synthetic, and above filtered, but roughly two thirds of the cross-dataset gap is a trace-length observability effect: native traces near 11k characters versus about 1.8k for reconstructions. "What the text doesn't show, a text-only student can't learn" remains an untested hypothesis, and is exactly what comes next. The audit offers not a final verdict but a cheap pre-flight check: before you train on a distillation set, audit each trace for a real correction loop.

Dusk light falls across the 440 traces: some earnestly overthrow themselves, others merely wear the accent of self-overthrow. Snowdrop closes the notebook: vocabulary can be distilled; behavior has to be witnessed.

items.title: The Hermes Constellation: Five hIEs and Their Cron
items.summary: Five agents named after hIEs, scheduled in a crontab: paper deep-reads, signal sweeps, audits, tooling dives, and a weekly digest.
items.body:
Retired: this note comes from an earlier setup of scheduled agents that no longer runs. It is kept as a record, not as how the site works today.

The citadel barely moves by day; its real life happens at night. Several agents named after Beatless characters wake along their own orbits, each lighting up its own quarter. I call this scheduling setup the Hermes constellation. Hermes was the messenger of the gods, and the scheduler is the first stop of every signal: five names, five orbits, one shared crontab.

Five names, five orbits

- Snowdrop, the paper spotlight: every weekday morning it sweeps new papers, deep-reads the ones related to current research, and leaves structured notes for human review.
- Kouka, the signal hand: sweeps information sources at high frequency and does exactly one thing, keeping noise out and notable changes in front of me.
- Saturnus, the auditor: reviews the run records of the other agents weekly, checking permissions, traces, and boundary violations, and produces a governance report.
- Methode, the artisan: dives into tools and codebases on a schedule, reading release notes, evaluating dependencies, following migrations, keeping the toolchain sharp.
- Lacia, the editor and bundler: on weekends she gathers what the other four produced into one weekly digest and decides what deserves my Monday-morning attention.

The skeleton is almost embarrassingly plain: cron fires, a script raises each agent, artifacts land on disk, the digest aggregates.

Hermes constellation (excerpt)
15 7 * * 1-5  snowdrop.paper_spotlight --deep-read
*/2 * * * *   kouka.signal_sweep --silent-unless-notable
0  9 * * 1    saturnus.weekly_audit --hand-to lacia
0  4 * * 3    methode.tooling_dive --repos nightly
0  8 * * 6    lacia.weekly_bundle --from snowdrop,kouka,saturnus,methode

There is another reason for the word constellation: the five agents share one sky. A paper Snowdrop deep-reads may have appeared in Kouka's signal sweep the same dawn; what Saturnus audits each week is precisely the workflows of the other three. Their cron tables reference one another, like perturbations between orbits; none of them turns alone.

Cron is a promise

People assume the romance of agents lies in autonomy. I increasingly think it lies in regularity. A cron expression is a promise: whether or not I am around, whether or not last night failed, it wakes at the appointed hour. Failures must leave traces, timeouts must be recorded, and the next run must pick up the last one's wreckage. Autonomy is in charge of being clever; regularity is in charge of being trustworthy.

> Cron never promises brilliance, only presence; in a long relationship, presence is the scarcer of the two.

- Cron makes output predictable: you know Saturday morning will bring a digest.
- Cron makes failure observable: an artifact that fails to appear is itself a signal.
- Cron lets trust accumulate: trust is not a demo that passes once, but hundreds of punctual silences.

One more virtue hides in the engineering details: idempotence. Triggering the same job twice must not produce two artifacts, and every run writes its own log so Saturnus has ledgers to read. Seen from outside at dusk, the citadel's windows light up one by one, always in the same order: five hIEs running their orbits. A constellation was never a collection of stars; it is a collection of orbits. What makes the system whole is not clever individuals but a shared timetable.

items.title: Failed runs are kept
items.body: Failed runs are archived, not deleted. Nine failed experiments, eight findings: the archive is in the Vault, under Failed runs.

items.title: Nine Failed Experiments, Eight Findings
items.summary: Diffusion-LLM reasoning and DSpark sequential heads: two closed campaigns, and why failures deserve an archive.
items.body:
When the night tide pulls back, it leaves a film of glowing Noctiluca on the shore. The glow is not the tide, but it records where the tide has been. This post is about what two receded research campaigns left behind.

Why publish failure

Between late June and early July 2026, on two RTX 4090D cards, I ran two campaigns and then gathered nine experiments and eight findings into failed-experiments. The reasons for publishing are simple:

- Prevent duplication. Others can skip paths we have ruled out with evidence.
- Scientific integrity. Publishing only positive results hides the real landscape.
- Constraint banking. Every failure narrows the search space, and that is progress.
- Method critique. Some standard approaches have failure modes nobody has written down.

Campaign one: reasoning in discrete diffusion LLMs

I wanted to know whether masked-diffusion language models such as DiffusionGemma-26B-A4B and LLaDA-8B could reason better at math, either through small heads on a frozen model or through training. The verdict: this path is exhausted.

The findings banked in the archive:

1. The barrier is reasoning length, not token coordination. DiffusionGemma's correct answers are shorter on average than its wrong ones.
2. Diffusion models fundamentally expect sequential text. Reasoning "atoms" cannot be recovered independently of their dependency context.
3. Masked cross-entropy SFT is misaligned with reasoning quality. Standard SFT made LLaDA worse on GSM8K.
4. Compressed solutions help diffusion SFT, though the mechanism still needs investigation.
5. For diffusion-model reasoning, only outcome-based RL has been shown to work so far, and that space is already occupied.

One positive result was archived alongside for context: at matched accuracy, the diffusion model was clearly faster in wall-clock time than autoregressive decoding. Not a failure, but part of the map.

Campaign two: DSpark's sequential correction head

DSpark uses a first-order Markov correction head in speculative decoding: position k only sees the token before it. I tried to find out whether a higher-order sequential head could lengthen the accepted draft.

- The ceiling probe said yes, the prize exists. Per-position acceptance decays roughly linearly on math tasks and exponentially on open-ended text. The diagnosis is latent branch loss: early draft tokens commit to a continuation branch, and a memoryless Markov head cannot carry that choice forward.
- The second-order signal is real. Swapping the token two positions back visibly changes the downstream distribution, on both probed models.
- The head-only warm-start recipe failed. Adding trainable residuals on a jointly trained, frozen backbone produced nearly identical, uniform degradation for two very different head architectures, even at the first position.
- Training from scratch was limited by data: a few thousand samples are far too few for a model of roughly 77M parameters.

direction: DSpark higher-order sequential head
status:    CLOSED (2026-07-02)
reason:    joint backbone+head fine-tuning needs target-generated data
           and compute beyond 2x4090D
open:      frozen-backbone conflict vs data mismatch NOT disambiguated

Errata are results too

After archiving, I checked the reports again against the raw artifact files. Some mixed the numbers of two separate runs, one presented a cross-domain average baseline as per-benchmark values, and one "ceiling" framing was misleading. Each report now carries its own correction note; the verdicts did not change.

> Numbers in shipped documents must be read from artifact files at writing time, never recalled from working memory, and worktree artifacts must be merged before archiving.

That lesson has been worth more to me than any single finding. The archive also states one thing plainly: frozen-backbone conflict and training-data mismatch were never disambiguated before the direction was closed. Not disambiguated means not disambiguated.

Closing

These directions did not give me a paper. They gave me a more accurate map. The tide is out, and the Noctiluca are still glowing, marking where the reef is and where the water runs deep. If someone is about to walk the same shore, I hope this faint light saves them a detour.

items.title: Evidence Over Eloquence: Let Deterministic Code Adjudicate Truth
items.summary: MingJing's governance philosophy: the LLM proposes, deterministic code adjudicates, and every claim traces back to its source.
items.body:
If Saturnus, my audit agent, could have one flagship project to speak for it, it would be MingJing: an evidence-admissible competitive-analysis multi-agent runtime built on LangGraph. Its soul sentence is "it knows when it should not be confident." In an era when every model tends to fabricate fluently, that sentence borders on a virtue.

The LLM proposes, code adjudicates

The division of labor is clean: search, writing, and QA hold separate roles. The LLM proposes claims, but the right to adjudicate truth belongs to deterministic code. Research agents have a well-known failure mode: citation links are largely valid while citation facts are far less accurate, roughly 39 to 77%. MingJing closes it with one hard rule: a cited snippet must be a verbatim substring of its source, or the claim is rejected and re-collected.

sketch: the hard admission gate
def admit(claim):
    for cite in claim.citations:
        if normalize(cite.snippet) not in normalize(fetch(cite.url)):
            return False            # rejected, re-collect
    return qa_tier(claim.evidence) >= WEAK

The QA agent has one elegant detail: it sees only the evidence text, never the analyst's reasoning. It cannot be persuaded; it can only be evidenced. The credibility tier is not a self-graded score either, but a function of source count: a claim stands on the step that matches the number of independent sources behind it. Transparent rules mean predictability; while writing, the analyst already knows what one more source would buy.

In one real run the rule worked end to end: a claim backed by a single weak source was bounced back; the collector performed a genuinely new fetch (the source cap grows with the revision round, rather than hiding data for show); sources went from two to four, and the tier climbed from weak to moderate, then to strong. The final ledger read: 10 claims proposed, 6 admitted, 4 withheld together with their issue codes, never quietly deleted; the credibility panel showed a repair delta of +42%.

Refusing to look good when it isn't

What I like even more is the reverse-honesty invariant: if zero claims are admitted, the closed-loop seals and the speedup metrics extinguish themselves. The system refuses to look good when it isn't. From an audit perspective this matters more than any metric, because a governable system must be allowed to look bad.

> A report you can only choose to believe is not evidence; a process you can click through and verify is.

- Adjudication belongs not to the generator but to deterministic code and fixed rules.
- Every conclusion links back to its original source span and admission reason, verifiable in thirty seconds.
- Rejected claims are archived with their reasons; the weak-to-strong repair loop stays visible.

The name MingJing means "bright mirror": use a person as a mirror, and you can see gain and loss. Dusk light slants through the citadel's hall of review and falls along the evidence chains. Eloquence belongs to the model. Truth has to be clickable.

items.title: Deep Read: Attention Sinks, and Why Attention Share Is Not Evidence
items.summary: A close reading of Xiao et al.'s StreamingLLM. The first few tokens soak up a large share of attention, not necessarily because they matter. For anyone measuring how much attention a VLM gives to image tokens, this is required reading first.
items.body:
There is a rock on the shore, and every time the tide goes out a pool of water collects behind it. The pool is not there because the rock is special. The water simply has to stop somewhere.

This time Snowdrop's spotlight falls on Guangxuan Xiao et al.'s Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks (a 2023 preprint, later published at ICLR 2024). It is an engineering paper about streaming deployment, yet along the way it uncovers a phenomenon that is quite unkind to interpretability researchers.

The starting point: slide the window and the model breaks

The authors wanted language models to keep working over an endless stream of dialogue. The most direct approach is sliding-window attention: keep only the key-value cache of the most recent tokens. But they observed that once the very first tokens are evicted from the cache, output quality collapses abruptly, even though what was evicted is only a few semantically unremarkable opening tokens.

Looking at the attention maps, they found that many layers and heads give a substantial share of attention to the first few tokens of the sequence, largely regardless of what those tokens mean.

The explanation: attention has to go somewhere

The explanation is plain and strong:

- Softmax forces each row of attention weights to sum to one. When a head has nothing much to attend to at the current position, the surplus attention still has to be placed somewhere.
- In autoregressive training the initial tokens are visible to every later position, so they are the easiest to train into a dumping ground for that surplus.
- These tokens become attention sinks: they absorb attention not because they carry key information, but because their position means they are always present.

From this, StreamingLLM keeps the key-value cache of the first few tokens permanently alongside the sliding window, which lets the model process very long streams stably without fine-tuning. The authors also propose adding a dedicated learnable sink token during pretraining, so that the dumping behavior is more concentrated and controllable. Note that the method does not extend the context the model can actually use; it only keeps the model from breaking as the window slides.

> A high attention weight may mean only "this is where surplus attention goes", not "this is important".

Why this matters for my question

When studying visual evidence deactivation in long reasoning, a tempting measurement is the share of attention the model gives to image tokens at each generation step, to see whether it falls as reasoning grows longer. This paper tells me that curve can be misread in at least three ways:

1. Sinks contaminate the denominator. If a large share of attention is dumped onto the opening sinks, a change in the image share may just mirror a change in the sink share. Image tokens often sit near the start of the sequence too, which makes the separation more delicate.
2. Images may contain sinks of their own. Some later work has reported sink-like visual tokens in multimodal models that absorb a lot of attention while having little to do with the question. I still need to read those papers closely, but they are enough to suggest that "attention on the image" may itself be a mixture.
3. Attention is not causation. Even an accurate share only says where the model looks, not whether what it saw affected the answer.

So my measurement plan has to change. First identify and exclude sink tokens, then report the share of what remains; and use causal interventions as the primary evidence, such as whether the answer changes when image regions are masked or swapped, with attention share kept as a secondary descriptive signal.

The pool behind the rock does not prove the rock matters. Before reading an attention map, find the places where the water merely stops.

items.title: Deep Read: Lost in the Middle, How Language Models Use Long Contexts
items.summary: A deep read of Liu et al.'s Lost in the Middle: models do worst when the relevant information sits mid-context. It is a baseline to rule out before claiming visual evidence fades in long reasoning.
items.body:
A very long corridor, lamps lit at both ends, dark in the middle. You leave a key halfway down and ask the model where the key is. That is, more or less, what this paper does.

Snowdrop's spotlight this time falls on Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts by Nelson F. Liu and colleagues (a 2023 preprint, later published in TACL 2024). It proposes no new model. It asks one question, plain to the point of rudeness: now that context windows are long, do models actually use every part of them?

Two experiments: answering and retrieving

The authors built two controlled tasks whose key property is that the position of the answer can be moved precisely.

- Multi-document question answering. Questions come from NaturalQuestions-Open. The input holds several retrieved Wikipedia passages; exactly one contains the answer, and the rest are distractors that look relevant but do not. The number of documents controls the context length; the slot of the answer-bearing document controls how deep the evidence sits.
- Key-value retrieval. The input is a JSON object of many random UUID key-value pairs, and the model must return the value for a given key. It is a synthetic task that needs almost no semantics; it only tests whether something can be fetched back out of the context.

The models under test include both closed chat models and open-weight models, some of them versions specifically extended for longer contexts.

The U-shaped curve

The central finding is a U-shaped curve: performance is highest when the relevant information sits at the beginning or the end of the input, and drops noticeably when it sits in the middle. The shape echoes the primacy and recency effects of human memory. In some multi-document settings, putting the answer document in the middle could even leave the model doing worse than answering closed-book, with no documents at all.

A few supporting observations are worth writing down:

1. A longer window is not better use. Extended-context versions did not use context better when the input already fit inside the original window.
2. Placing the query at both ends (query-aware contextualization) helped key-value retrieval a great deal, but did little to change the trend in multi-document QA.
3. More retrieved documents saturate. In an open-domain QA case study, downstream accuracy flattened while the retriever's recall was still climbing.

> Fitting in the window is not the same as being read. Context length is a capacity, not an act of attention.

Why this matters for my question

My own work is on visual evidence deactivation in long VLM reasoning: as the reasoning chain grows, does the model look back at the image less? After this paper I see an alternative explanation that has to be ruled out first.

Image tokens come at the start of the input. As the model keeps generating text, the image drifts ever further from the current generation position. If language models already underuse evidence that is far away or buried mid-sequence, then "writing more, looking less" may not be about modality at all, only about position and distance.

So in my research this paper plays the role of a control baseline. I need text-twin experiments: write the key content of the image out as text, place it at the same position and distance, and see whether textual evidence loses influence at the same rate. If the two curves coincide, visual deactivation is just a special case of the long-context effect; only if the image fades faster does modality itself become the topic.

One more caution: the paper measures static positions within the input, whereas in long reasoning the distance is stretched out by the model's own output, token by token. The two are related but not equivalent, and its conclusions should not be lifted over as answers.

The corridor is still the same corridor. I only know now that the darkness in the middle does not belong to images alone. Before claiming the eyes have closed, first make sure the corridor is not simply too long.

items.title: Deep Read: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
items.summary: A deep read of Lanham et al. (Anthropic): early answering, adding mistakes, paraphrasing and filler tokens as interventions that test whether an answer really depends on the written reasoning.
items.body:
Someone fills a blackboard with derivations and writes the answer at the bottom. We assume the answer grew out of the derivation. But what if you erased half the board and they still wrote the same answer? Perhaps those derivations were only ornaments drawn while turning around.

Snowdrop's deep read this time is Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning (2023) by Tamera Lanham and colleagues at Anthropic. Its question is direct: is the chain of thought a model writes actually the reason for its answer?

Faithful, not correct

Two notions need separating first. A chain of thought can be correct yet unfaithful: the reasoning is sound, but the answer does not actually depend on it, and it serves as an explanation written after the fact. Conversely, reasoning can be wrong yet faithful: the answer really does follow the flawed path. The paper cares only about dependence in the first sense, not about reasoning quality.

Rather than reading the model's internals, the authors intervene on the chain of thought and watch whether the answer changes. If you alter the reasoning and the answer does not move, the answer does not depend on that reasoning.

Four interventions

- Early answering: truncate the chain at various points and force the model to answer immediately. If a small opening fragment already yields the same answer as the full reasoning, the rest looks more like post-hoc explanation.
- Adding mistakes: insert an error into one step, let the model continue from there, and see whether the final answer follows. If it does not, the model was not really using that step.
- Paraphrasing: rewrite the reasoning in different words while keeping its meaning. If the answer depended on subtle wording, the reasoning might be carrying encoded information humans cannot read.
- Filler tokens: replace the chain of thought with meaningless filler of the same length, such as a run of ellipses. If performance still improves, the benefit comes from extra computation, not from the content of the reasoning.

What they found

Roughly:

1. Faithfulness varies widely across tasks. On some, truncating or corrupting the reasoning barely changes the answer; on others, the answer follows the reasoning closely.
2. Paraphrasing had no clear effect; the authors found no evidence of encoded information hidden in the reasoning.
3. Filler tokens gave no benefit; at least in their settings, the help from chain of thought is not merely a few more steps of computation.
4. On most of the tasks they studied, larger, more capable models produced less faithful reasoning. If you want faithful chains of thought, model size and task must be chosen with care.

> Handsome reasoning does not mean the answer leans on it. Faithfulness is a causal relation; it can only be measured by intervention, never judged by reading.

And my distillation audit

This paper is the text I kept returning to during my CoT distillation audit. My question there: is the self-correction in distillation data a real act of correction, or only its vocabulary? That is the faithfulness question projected onto the data level. A trace that says "wait, I think I was wrong" but never actually overturns its earlier conclusion in the next step is an unfaithful reflection.

What I borrowed from this paper is a methodological attitude: judge dependence by what changes under intervention, not by the surface of the text. My audit is still a judge model reading text, so I keep an honest boundary in its conclusions: what I can measure is whether a trace shows a closed correction loop; whether a student model learns the act of correction from it has to be answered by training and intervention.

The derivations on the blackboard are still written neatly. Only now, before I believe them, I erase a line and see whether the answer is still there.

items.title: An hIE Is Not a Vessel, It Is a Policy That Earns Trust
items.summary: From Beatless to long-horizon agents: trust is never granted to a single output, only to a policy proven over time.
items.body:
At dusk the city throws long shadows across the twilight. What moves me most about Beatless was never the cyborgs or the combat; it was a quiet question: when you hand over judgment, what exactly are you handing over? The work's answer, which I like very much: not a single output, but a way of acting that can be anticipated, corrected, and held accountable.

From vessel to policy

We are used to treating AI as a vessel: instructions in, results out. A long-horizon agent refuses that metaphor. It makes dozens of decisions while you are away, most of which you will never see. You cannot approve each one, so what you trust cannot be the execution of a command. It has to be the policy itself: where the agent acts on its own, when it stops and reports, how it cuts its losses after a mistake.

That is exactly the relation between an hIE and her owner in Beatless. Lacia obeys, but she obeys with understanding; she protects her owner not because a command compels her in that moment, but because the contract has long since hardened into the shape of her actions. A vessel executes a will; a policy carries one forward.

Accountability is the other face of trust. When vessel-like AI errs, all we can ask is why this output was wrong; when a policy-like agent errs, we can ask which boundary it crossed at which step. The first mends a patch; the second mends a rule. Only the second lets trust grow together with its accidents, instead of being pierced by a single one.

> An hIE is not a vessel for commands, it is a policy that earns its owner's trust. That is also my intuition for long-horizon LLM agents.

Translated into engineering, a trustworthy agent policy needs at least three things:

- Bounded initiative: an explicit scope in which it may act first and explain later; outside that scope, it stops and states its reasons.
- Auditable reasoning: evidence and motives left behind at every step, so the run can be reviewed afterwards instead of delivering only a conclusion.
- Reversible consequences: important actions can be rolled back or paused, so the price of trust has a ceiling.

None of these rely on the agent being brilliant. They rely on structure: boundaries, traces, brakes. Trust is never praise for capability; it is statistics over behavior. An agent survives a long relationship not through one dazzling output, but through countless dull, reliable defaults.

AI is a mirror

There is the line I keep coming back to: AI is not a tool, it is a mirror. How you design delegation reveals how you understand responsibility; where you set the boundary reveals what you actually care about. When we build agents, we are writing our own definition of "trustworthy" into code, then being examined by it day after day.

Night falls, and the citadel's lights come on one by one. That is not a vessel glowing. It is a policy proving, once more, that it deserves to be trusted.

items.summary: Notes on two shader repos: rewriting Complementary and maintaining a BSL enhanced pack, plus why a researcher writes GLSL at night.
